description: Somos ERIS, estudiantes de Ingeniería de Sistemas e Industrial enfocados en crear soluciones innovadoras con datos de la NASA. Contamos con conocimientos en programación, análisis de datos y gestión de proyectos. Buscamos integrantes con habilidades en agricultura, ciencias de la Tierra, estadística y análisis de datos que quieran innovar y aportar soluciones de impacto.
summary:
Cusco Environmental Trends is a proposed web platform that uses historical NASA Earth observation datasets to investigate how environmental variables changed across the Cusco region from 2021 through 2025. It addresses five practical questions: what changed, where it changed, whether it increased or decreased, by how much, and whether the observed trend is statistically significant. The system is intended for students, educators, researchers, and local decision-makers who need understandable, traceable findings without performing every statistical calculation themselves.
The first version prioritizes monthly precipitation and near-surface air temperature in four geographically contrasting study areas. Soil moisture and vegetation (NDVI) are planned extensions if time permits. Results will first be cleaned and validated in Excel and independently checked in Python before being incorporated into the web dashboard. All conclusions must be linked to the original dataset, time interval, geographic area, units, and statistical evidence.
details:
Environmental change is spatially uneven. Cusco combines high-altitude grasslands, inter-Andean valleys, urban and agricultural basins, and humid cloud-forest environments. A single regional average can conceal opposite trends in different locations. Although NASA tools support downloading time series, users still need to clean data, account for seasonality, apply statistical tests, and interpret uncertainty. This project connects those steps to an accessible public interface.

General objective

Develop and validate a prototype web platform that identifies which environmental variables are changing, where, in which direction, at what rate, and with what statistical evidence in selected areas of Cusco using NASA data.

Specific objectives

·  Document four environmental variables and four contrasting geographic study areas.

· Build monthly time series for 2021–2025, using 2026 only when comparable complete data are available.

·  Estimate linear trends, Mann–Kendall significance, and Sen’s slope; report uncertainty and sample size.

·  Cross-check spreadsheet calculations against Python and, where available, independent station records.

·  Provide a public-facing dashboard with understandable explanations and optional registered-user features.

The proposed sampling approach uses approximately 0.5° × 0.5° areas around the reference points. Coordinates, boundaries, elevations, and whether each source supports the same extraction geometry must be verified before analysis.

4. How the Solution Works

· A researcher selects a variable, study area, and analysis period.

· The data pipeline imports the relevant monthly NASA time series and preserves its source metadata.

·   Quality checks identify missing values, duplicates, inconsistent units, and unusual observations.

·   The analysis calculates seasonal anomalies, change rates, uncertainty, and trend significance.

· The dashboard displays the main conclusion, a time-series chart, a geographic comparison, and the underlying evidence.

· An optional expanded view offers detailed statistics, seasonality, and downloadable validated data.

The main result should explicitly answer the five challenge questions in plain English. Example template (not an actual result): “In [area], [variable] [increased/decreased] by an estimated [rate and unit] per year during [period]. The 95% confidence interval was [lower, upper], and the trend [was/was not] statistically significant (p = [value]).”

5. Data Preparation and Statistical Methodology

Stage A — Acquisition and quality control

· Download the selected monthly products and retain untouched originals and source URLs.

·  Standardize timestamps, area boundaries, units, and missing-value conventions.

· Flag outliers; compare results with and without flagged values instead of deleting them automatically.

· Do not fill missing months without a documented, defensible method.

· Maintain a change log and a data dictionary covering source, version, resolution, and transformations.

Suggested interpretation rule from the original plan: a trend is “significant” when regression and Mann–Kendall both give p < 0.05 with the same direction; borderline or discordant outcomes are described as suggestive or inconclusive. Failure to reject a trend test does not prove that no change occurred. Serial correlation can make naïve p-values too optimistic; seasonality, autocorrelation, ties, and short time coverage must be considered before making scientific claims.

For Mann–Kendall, S is the sum of sign(xⱼ − xᵢ) across all i < j. With no ties, Var(S) = n(n−1)(2n+5)/18. A continuity-corrected Z score and two-sided normal probability give the approximate p-value. Sen’s slope is the median of all pairwise slopes. Use the actual time spacing when months are missing.

The primary evidence for the MVP is one complete end-to-end consultation based on real, reproducible data. All data presented as simulated, illustrative, or reference-only must be labeled accordingly. A 60-month window describes observed change over 2021–2025, not necessarily long-term climate change.

7. Dashboard and User Experience

Public interface

·Immediate access to variable, area, and date selectors without mandatory sign-up.

·  One concise result statement answering what, where, direction, magnitude, and significance.

·  Monthly time-series chart with trend overlay and comparison across study areas.

· Dataset citation, time span, units, valid observations, and a clear methodological note.

Registered-user extensions

· More comparisons and up to four visualizations.

·  Seasonal-cycle and area-by-year heatmap views.

· Detailed statistical table including Sen slope, Mann–Kendall p-value, and R².

· Exportable results and user history, if implementation time allows.

The supplied HTML prototype uses generated demonstration series and a simulated registration dialog. It should not be presented as a live NASA data feed, a production authentication system, or validated scientific findings. The redesign should prioritize a readable visual hierarchy, honest data-status labeling, and a consistent mapping from each statistic to its explanation.

8. Technology, AI Use, and Project Workflow

Proposed implementation: a responsive HTML/CSS/JavaScript dashboard, CSV or JSON results exported from the validated analysis, Excel for the initial calculation workflow, and Python for independent verification. Authentication may use a managed service in a later phase. No production deployment stack, data pipeline automation, or verified user database is claimed by this document.

AI tools may assist with writing, translation, interface prototyping, and code review, but data processing choices, statistical outputs, citations, and final interpretations must be checked by the team. AI-generated examples must never be substituted for downloaded measurements.

9. Eight Development Stages and Hackathon Priorities

1. Research and data collection

Confirm challenge requirements, datasets, variables, geographic areas and monthly coverage; document provenance.

2. Cleaning and preparation

Preserve originals, normalize units, handle gaps and flag anomalies; create analysis-ready tables.

3. Statistical analysis

Calculate anomalies, slopes, significance, confidence intervals and comparisons in Excel.

4. Verification and validation

Cross-check with Python, KNMI and available ground observations; resolve inconsistencies.

5. Web interface development

Build public queries, results, charts and optional user features.

6. Statistical integration

Import validated CSV/JSON or implement equivalent computations; compare results against Excel.

7. System testing

Test every available area-variable combination, incomplete periods, chart readability and user comprehension.

8. Documentation and presentation

Provide methods, sources, evidence, limitations, screenshots and a 30-second English pitch.

Hackathon MVP for November 14–15, 2026: prioritize precipitation and temperature across four areas (eight monthly series). Add soil moisture and NDVI only if time permits. The pitch should cover the problem, the tool, one verified real result, and why it matters. Future versions may add longer histories, additional locations, predictive modeling, agricultural applications, and automated refreshes.

10. Expected Benefits, Risks, and Future Work

· Accessibility: turn technical satellite series into understandable local evidence.

· Transparency: expose the dataset, geography, time span, method, and uncertainty for every finding.

· Reproducibility: use documented data transformations and independent calculation checks.

· Regional relevance: compare environmental behavior across distinct altitudinal and ecological zones.

Principal limitations include the short 2021–2025 interval, spatial averaging in complex mountain terrain, delayed availability of some finalized precipitation products, cloud contamination in vegetation products, serial correlation, and limited hackathon development time. The application should avoid causal or agricultural recommendations unless supported by separate evidence.
